extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of classical political economy; economists and historians
extracted.subtask_description: Analysis/exposition from a classical political-economy treatise (discussion of how improvement, market extent, transportability, and regulations affect prices of various 'rude produce' and the value of precious metals).

rubrics_metrics.name: General effect of improvement on prices
rubrics_metrics.description: Though the real price of this sort of rude produce, therefore, naturally tends to rise in the progress of improvement, yet, according as different accidents happen ... it may happen sometimes even to fall, sometimes to continue the same, in very different periods of improvement, and sometimes to rise more or less in the same period.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Improvement generally pushes up real prices of rude produce, but accidents and contingencies can make the outcome variable; expect rise on average but allow for exceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appendage goods limited by primary produce
rubrics_metrics.description: There are some sorts of rude produce which nature has rendered a kind of appendages to other sorts; so that the quantity of the one which any country can afford, is necessarily limited by that of the other. The quantity of wool or of raw hides ... is necessarily limited by the number of great and small cattle that are kept in it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a commodity is an appendage (byproduct) of another, its available quantity and prospects depend on the primary good (e.g., wool/hides depend on cattle numbers); plan expectations accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Market extent and transportability determine price reaction
rubrics_metrics.description: The same causes ... raise the price of butcher’s meat, should have the same effect, it may be thought, upon the prices of wool and raw hides ... But the extent of their respective markets is commonly extremely different. The market for butcher’s meat is almost everywhere confined to the country which produces it. The market for wool and raw hides ... is very seldom confined to the country which produces them. They can easily be transported to distant countries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a commodity's market is local (poorly transportable), domestic improvement will expand demand and raise price more than for easily transportable commodities sold on wide markets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Local vs international markets cause differential price dynamics
rubrics_metrics.description: The market for the carcase being in the rude state of society confined always to the country which produces it, must necessarily be extended in proportion to the improvement and population of that country. But the market for the wool and the hides ... often extending to the whole commercial world, it can very seldom be enlarged in the same proportion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect prices of locally-traded goods to rise with domestic improvement; internationally-traded raw materials will not necessarily rise similarly because their market size is set by global demand.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relative component values depend on cultivation level
rubrics_metrics.description: In countries ill cultivated, and therefore but thinly inhabited, the price of the wool and the hide bears always a much greater proportion to that of the whole beast, than in countries where, improvement and population being further advanced, there is more demand for butcher’s meat.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The share of a commodity's parts in total value shifts with agricultural development (e.g., wool/hide share higher in uncultivated regions). Use relative prices as indicators of cultivation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improvement raises carcass price more than byproduct prices
rubrics_metrics.description: Though, in the progress of improvement and population, the price of the whole beast necessarily rises, yet the price of the carcase is likely to be much more affected by this rise than that of the wool and the hide.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing price changes for multi-part commodities, weight the carcass/meat component more heavily in response to domestic improvement than byproducts with broader markets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trade regulations can artificially alter natural prices
rubrics_metrics.description: This degradation ... has accordingly been the effect of violence and artifice. First, of the absolute prohibition of exporting wool from England: secondly, of the permission of importing it from Spain, duty free: thirdly, of the prohibition of exporting it from Ireland ... In consequence of these regulations, the market for English wool ... has been confined to the home market.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legal restrictions (export bans, preferential imports, regional trade constraints) can confine markets and depress or distort prices relative to what natural market forces would produce; examine statutes and duties when explaining price anomalies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distribution of price among parts indifferent to landlords/farmers if total maintained
rubrics_metrics.description: In what manner this price is to be divided upon the different parts of the beast, is indifferent to the landlords and farmers, provided it is all paid to them. ... Their interest as landlords and farmers cannot be much affected by such regulations, though their interest as consumers may, by the rise in the price of provisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Landlord/farmer welfare depends on total receipts from cattle; redistributions among parts (wool vs carcass) matter less to them than to consumers or to producers in regions specialized in one part.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of price-falls on unimproved economies
rubrics_metrics.description: In an unimproved and uncultivated country, where the greater part of the lands could be applied to no other purpose but the feeding of cattle ... The fall in the price of the wool and the hide would not in this case raise the price of the carcase ... The whole price of cattle would fall, and along with it both the rent and the profit of all those lands of which cattle was the principal produce.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In agrarian economies specialized in pastoral land-use, price drops for byproducts can reduce total livestock value and depress land rent and profits; policy affecting byproduct prices can thus have deep local effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geographical supply limits raise prices with expanding demand (fish example)
rubrics_metrics.description: The quantity of fish that is brought to market ... is limited by the local situation of the country, by the proximity or distance of its different provinces from the sea ... A market which, from requiring only one thousand, comes to require annually ten thousand ton of fish, can seldom be supplied, without employing more than ten times the quantity of labour ... The real price of this commodity, therefore, naturally rises in the progress of improvement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For goods constrained by local geography or resource location, large increases in demand require disproportionate inputs and raise real price as societies improve.

rubrics_metrics.name: Precious metals abundance determined by purchasing power and mine fertility
rubrics_metrics.description: The quantity of the precious metals ... seems to depend upon two different circumstances; first, upon its power of purchasing, upon the state of its industry ... and, secondly, upon the fertility or barrenness of the mines which may happen at any particular time to supply the commercial world.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret changes in gold/silver quantities by separating domestic purchasing power effects (wealth, ability to buy) from exogenous supply shocks from mines; both affect nominal and real values differently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish nominal from real effects of metal abundance
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the one or the other of those two events may happen to take place, is of very little importance to the real wealth and prosperity of the world, to the real value of the annual produce ... Its nominal value, the quantity of gold and silver by which this annual produce could be expressed or represented, would, no doubt, be very different; but its real value, the real quantity of labour which it could purchase or command, would be precisely the same.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not equate increases in money supply (gold/silver) with increases in real wealth; analyze effects on nominal prices separately from real purchasing power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Money price levels are not direct indicators of civilization
rubrics_metrics.description: The greater part of the writers ... seem to have considered the low money price of corn, and of goods in general ... as a proof ... of the poverty and barbarism of the country ... I shall only observe at present, that the high value of the precious metals can be no proof of the poverty or barbarism of any particular country ... It is a proof only of the barrenness of the mines which happened at that time to supply the commercial world.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid inferring social development solely from absolute money prices; instead consider relative prices among goods and underlying metal supplies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relative prices of specific goods indicate state of improvement
rubrics_metrics.description: But though the low money price, either of goods in general, or of corn in particular, be no proof of the poverty or barbarism of the times, the low money price of some particular sorts of goods, such as cattle, poultry, game of all kinds, etc. in proportion to that of corn, is a most decisive one. It clearly demonstrates ... the uncultivated and unimproved state of the far greater part of the lands of the country.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use relative price comparisons (e.g., animal products vs corn) to infer land use intensity, population density, and degree of agricultural improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniform vs differential price rise diagnoses
rubrics_metrics.description: Any rise in the money price of goods which proceeded altogether from the degradation of the value of silver, would affect all sorts of goods equally ... But the rise in the price of provisions ... does not affect all sorts of provisions equally.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If price rises are uniform across goods, suspect monetary (metal) effects; if rises are uneven, search for specific supply/demand or production-structure causes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interconnected effects of agricultural improvement on food prices
rubrics_metrics.description: The extension of improvement and cultivation, as it necessarily raises more or less, in proportion to the price of corn, that of every sort of animal food, so it as necessarily lowers that of, I believe, every sort of vegetable food ... If, in the progress of improvement, therefore, the real price of one species of food necessarily rises, that of another as necessarily falls; and it becomes a matter of more nicety to judge how far the rise in the one may be compensated by the fall in the other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing welfare or wage adjustments, consider offsetting price movements between animal and vegetable foods due to changes in land use and crop introduction (e.g., potatoes, maize, turnips).

rubrics_metrics.name: Policy implications depend on cause of price rise
rubrics_metrics.description: It may, too, be of some use to the public, in regulating the pecuniary reward of some of its inferior servants. If this rise in the price of some sorts of provisions be owing to a fall in the value of silver, their pecuniary reward ... ought certainly to be augmented in proportion ... But if this rise of price is owing to the increased value, in consequence of the improved fertility of the land ... it becomes a much nicer matter to judge ... whether it ought to be augmented at all.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public policy (wage adjustments, social judgments) must distinguish whether price increases stem from monetary depreciation or from real improvement in land productivity; the appropriate response differs substantially.
